title: Imapro Corp. v. The Queen (1992 TCC) SR&ED Decision
subject: Federal Court (Trial Division) appeal on how building construction and upkeep costs should be allocated to SR&ED.
keyPhrase: Imapro Corp v The Queen 1992 TCC
summary: Imapro Corp. v. The Queen, [1992] 2 C.T.C. 298, is a Federal Court—Trial Division decision on SR&ED expenditures under the Income Tax Act for Canadian corporations. The Court allowed a reasonable 47.3 per cent floor-area apportionment of capital construction costs for common and administrative areas, but held that current common-area upkeep costs were not directly attributable to SR&ED.
metaDescription: Review the landmark 1992 TCC SR&ED decision in Imapro Corp. v. The Queen ([1992] 2 C.T.C. 298) from the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and the Taxpayer's Claim

The decision of the Federal Court—Trial Division (McGillis J., September 25, 1992) in Imapro Corp. v. The Queen, [1992] 2 C.T.C. 298, also reported as Imapro Corporation v. The Queen, 92 DTC 6487 and Imapro Corp. v. Canada, [1992] 2 C.T.C. 298, stands as a foundational Canadian judicial authority governing the statutory boundaries of deductible Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) expenditures and Investment Tax Credit (ITC) eligibility under the Income Tax Act (Canada) (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). In this appeal brought under subsection 172(2) of the ITA before the Federal Court—Trial Division, the corporate taxpayer, Imapro Corporation, an Ottawa-based Canadian-controlled private corporation engaged in the research and development, manufacturing and sales of computer graphics and related equipment, sought to deduct as SR&ED expenditures for its 1987 and 1988 taxation years a 47.3 per cent portion of the capital construction costs and of the current maintenance and upkeep costs of the common and administrative areas of the single multi-purpose building it constructed between September 1987 and February 1988, with corresponding ITCs.

In filing its income tax returns, the taxpayer claimed investment tax credits of $309,962 (of which $61,992 were refundable) for 1987 and $743,813 (of which $520,635 were refundable) for 1988, and in early 1989 filed an amended 1987 return claiming additional investment tax credits of $211,022; in claiming its SR&ED expenditures, it apportioned 47.3 per cent of the total construction and current expenditures of its building to SR&ED, on the theory that the research and development area occupied 1,372.5 of the building's 2,902 square metres, or 47.3 per cent. The taxpayer contended that the 1988 transitional provision applied because it had entered into a written obligation on June 10, 1987 (before June 18, 1987) to construct the building and had completed it before 1990, that the Act permits the apportionment of both current and capital expenditures between the SR&ED and other areas of a building, that its 1988 current expenditures for the common areas were "directly attributable" to the provision of premises for SR&ED under clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(B) of the ITA and subsection 2900(3) of the ITR, and that the capital expenditures claimed were incurred for and all or substantially all attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister of National Revenue (then administering the Income Tax Act through the Department of National Revenue, a predecessor of today's Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)) reassessed the taxpayer's 1987 taxation year and assessed its 1988 taxation year on October 17, 1989, disallowing SR&ED capital expenditures for building construction costs of $259,379 (1987) and $140,053 (1988) relating to the common and administrative areas, SR&ED current expenditures of $9,714 (1988) for the light, power, water, maintenance, property taxes and telephone costs of the common areas, and $5,680 (1987) of current expenditures that did not reconcile with the ledger accounts, on the basis that the common and administrative areas were not used solely for SR&ED purposes; the Minister confirmed the assessments on September 12, 1990. At trial, the Crown's challenge rested on statutory interpretation under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations. Specifically, the Crown maintained that the transitional provision did not cover Imapro's circumstances, that the Department of Finance's written confirmation to Imapro and Interpretation Bulletin IT-151R3 were erroneous, and that the Act contains no provision permitting the apportionment of expenditures, so that expenditures must be allowed in their totality or disallowed; alternatively, it argued that the current expenditures for the common areas were not directly related to the provision of premises for SR&ED and that the capital expenditures were not all or substantially all attributable to SR&ED.

Furthermore, the dispute did not concern headcount, wage, or other financial prorating ratios: Imapro apportioned its building costs by floor area, 47.3 per cent of the building being used exclusively for research and development, and the Department itself had allowed the SR&ED capital and current expenditures for the research and development area on that basis, consistent with Interpretation Bulletin IT-151R3, which states that a reasonable portion of the cost of a building built partly for SR&ED can qualify as a capital expenditure on SR&ED. The disallowance was confined to the 47.3 per cent portion of costs relating to the common areas (such as reception, lunchroom, washrooms, hallways, shipping and receiving, and electrical, mechanical and garbage rooms) and the general administrative area serving all sectors of the company; the concept of "overhead on overhead" was not at issue in the case.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The legal dispute in Imapro Corp. v. The Queen operates within the statutory architecture of section 37 (in particular subparagraph 37(7)(c)(ii), and paragraph 37(7)(f) with its transitional provision enacted in 1988) of the Income Tax Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations. Under paragraphs 37(1)(a) and (b) of the ITA, as they applied to the 1987 and 1988 taxation years, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada could deduct current and capital expenditures on SR&ED; clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A) limited such expenditures to those incurred for and all or substantially all attributable to the prosecution, or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution, of SR&ED in Canada (a phrase the Department interpreted in Interpretation Bulletin IT-151 as at least 90%, a figure the Court, citing Wood v. M.N.R., treated as a departmental assessing policy rather than a mathematical rule), while clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(B) further limited current expenditures to those "directly attributable," as determined by regulation, to the prosecution of SR&ED or to the provision of such premises, facilities, or equipment.

Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations supplies the precise substantive and cost-accounting definitions required to operationalize section 37 of the ITA. First, subsection 2900(1) of the ITR (subsequently consolidated into subsection 248(1) of the ITA) defines SR&ED as systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis—encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement—while explicitly excluding market research, sales promotion, quality control, routine testing, research in the social sciences or humanities, commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, and style changes. Second, subsection 2900(2) of the ITR prescribes three categories of current expenditures as "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED: under paragraph 2900(2)(a), the cost of materials consumed or transformed in such prosecution; under paragraph 2900(2)(b), where an employee directly undertakes, supervises, or supports such prosecution, the portion of salary or wages and related benefits that can reasonably be considered to relate thereto; and under paragraph 2900(2)(c), other expenditures, or portions thereof, that are directly related to such prosecution and that would not have been incurred had such prosecution not occurred.

Third, subsection 2900(3) of the ITR prescribes two categories of current expenditures as "directly attributable" to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Paragraph 2900(3)(a) covers the cost of the maintenance and upkeep of such premises, facilities, or equipment (where those assets meet the "all or substantially all" dedication threshold), while paragraph 2900(3)(b) encompasses other expenditures, or portions thereof, that are directly related to the provision of such premises, facilities, or equipment and that would not have been incurred had such premises, facilities, or equipment not existed. Subsequent to the taxation years at issue in Imapro Corp., Parliament enacted subsection 37(8) of the ITA and subsection 2900(4) of the ITR, introducing the optional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method as a simplified statutory alternative to the Traditional Method for computing SR&ED overhead expenditures. Under the Traditional Method, however, taxpayers continue to claim actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661, governed directly by the statutory tests adjudicated in Imapro Corp. v. The Queen.
The Court's Final Holding and Jurisprudential Legacy

The Federal Court—Trial Division allowed the appeal in part, with costs, and returned the matter to the Minister for reassessment, holding that the transitional provision, interpreted according to its object and spirit, applied to Imapro; that the 1988 current expenditures for the maintenance and upkeep of the common areas were properly disallowed because a 47.3 per cent portion is neither "all or substantially all" attributable nor "directly attributable" to SR&ED within clauses 37(7)(c)(ii)(A) and (B) of the ITA and subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations; and that the 47.3 per cent portion of the capital construction costs of the common and administrative areas claimed for 1987 and 1988 was a reasonable apportionment and ought to have been allowed. The Court emphasized that the words "directly attributable" must be read in their context, bearing in mind that the previous wording of the Act was "wholly attributable," and that evidence that SR&ED employees used the common areas, and that those areas would have been smaller without the SR&ED sector, did not establish that the current maintenance and upkeep expenditures were directly attributable to SR&ED. Consequently, while the Court accepted that the Act contemplates the apportionment of expenditures between SR&ED and other uses of a building, a 47.3 per cent floor-area share of current common-area expenditures used only partially by R&D personnel did not qualify, whereas a reasonable apportionment of capital construction costs for common and administrative areas that are integral to, and routinely and regularly used by, the research and development sector was permitted.

In contemporary Canadian tax practice, Imapro Corp. v. The Queen (92 DTC 6487; [1992] 2 C.T.C. 298) is cited in Section 5.1.1 (Common areas) of the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy in support of the position that the cost of maintaining and upkeeping common areas is not directly related to the provision of premises or facilities for SR&ED. The decision is one of the authorities the CRA relies on in administering the "directly related" test for common-area costs; the CRA's broader two-pronged "directly related" and "incremental" tests and its disallowance of "overhead on overhead" are developed in the CRA's own policy rather than in the reasoning in Imapro, which addressed the construction and upkeep costs of a multi-purpose building.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
Failure to Satisfy the "Directly Related" Test and the Prohibition on "Overhead on Overhead"

The legal deficiency identified in Imapro Corp. with respect to the current expenditures was the failure to establish that the 47.3 per cent portion of the maintenance and upkeep costs of the common areas was all or substantially all attributable, or directly attributable, to the provision of premises for SR&ED; the CRA's current policy frames the related requirement as a direct connection between the claimed expenditure and the prosecution of SR&ED. Under general financial and managerial accounting conventions, overhead refers broadly to indirect expenses required to operate an enterprise that cannot be conveniently traced to a single cost object. Under section 37 of the ITA and section 2900 of the ITR, however, general accounting overhead is not automatically allowable for tax credit or pool deduction purposes. To satisfy the "directly related" statutory test under paragraph 2900(2)(c) or paragraph 2900(3)(b) of the ITR, an expenditure must connect directly—with no intervening step or intermediary—to at least one of the three elements identified in the CRA's policy: the SR&ED work itself, the SR&ED staff performing the work, or the machinery and equipment used by staff to perform the SR&ED.

The taxpayer's claim in Imapro did not involve expenditures connected to SR&ED only through an intermediary organizational function or secondary cost pool, a structural defect that the CRA's current policy, not the Imapro decision, defines as "overhead on overhead". Specifically, when a non-technical employee provides direct clerical or logistical support to the SR&ED effort (where such tasks do not fall within direct engineering support under paragraph 2900(2)(b)), the portion of that support employee's salary or wages directly linked and incremental to the SR&ED work is claimable as SR&ED overhead on Line 360 of Form T661. However, the related employee benefits of that support employee, or the corporate costs of developing an employee benefits program for SR&ED personnel, have only an indirect link to the SR&ED work because the employee's salary or the human resources function operates as an intervening step. By the same legal logic, general corporate legal services, employee relations, review and approval of SR&ED budgets, and cost-control administration are disqualified because an administrative or corporate management layer intervenes between the cost and the technical experimentation. Interest expenses on corporate borrowing and professional fees paid to prepare SR&ED tax claims are instead prescribed expenditures under Section 4.8 of the CRA's policy: they earn no ITCs, although interest can enter the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to the extent that the borrowed money is used to pay SR&ED expenditures.
Failure to Prove Incrementality ("But-For" Causation) for Premises, Facilities, and Equipment

The second statutory issue relevant to Imapro Corp. involves the requirement in subsection 2900(3) of the ITR, as it then read, that current expenditures directly attributable to the provision of premises be either the cost of maintenance and upkeep of such premises, facilities, or equipment, or other expenditures directly related to such provision that would not have been incurred had such premises, facilities, or equipment not existed; the CRA now also applies a parallel incremental test under paragraph 2900(2)(c) to expenditures related to the prosecution of SR&ED. In Imapro, the Court did not articulate a "but-for" or exclusivity standard; it held that evidence that SR&ED employees used the common areas, and that those areas would logically have been about one-half smaller without the research and development sector, did not establish that their current maintenance and upkeep costs were directly attributable to SR&ED.

The taxpayer failed this requirement only with respect to the $9,714 of 1988 current expenditures for the light, power, water, maintenance, property taxes and telephone costs of the common areas; equipment maintenance contracts and waste disposal were not at issue in the case. Where, as in Imapro, a corporation operates a single multi-purpose building housing sales, service, manufacturing, administrative, and research and development sectors, a 47.3 per cent share of the maintenance and upkeep costs of common areas (such as reception, the lunchroom, washrooms, hallways, and shipping and receiving areas) does not meet the "all or substantially all" threshold, nor is it "directly attributable" to SR&ED under subsection 2900(3) of the ITR, even though SR&ED employees use those areas regularly. Similarly, although the point was not decided in Imapro Corp., the CRA's policy (Section 3.2.1) takes the position that a fixed-cost maintenance contract on machinery, laboratory apparatus, or computer hardware generally fails the incremental test for SR&ED overhead and other expenditures. Because the periodic fee under a fixed-price service agreement remains constant irrespective of whether the equipment is used for commercial tasks, sits idle, or is deployed in intensive SR&ED trials, the cost is fixed and would have been incurred even if the SR&ED prosecution had not occurred.

Furthermore, temporal alignment is essential to proving incrementality for ancillary costs such as waste and scrap disposal. When experimental trials generate scrap materials or hazardous waste, disposal costs qualify only if incurred during the active prosecution of SR&ED; once the SR&ED activity that produced the scrap has finished, subsequent waste disposal costs are no longer considered directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED. Taxpayers must also distinguish capital expenditures from incremental operating expenses: expenditures of a capital nature, such as equipment purchases, do not qualify as SR&ED overhead, whereas incremental variable costs to operate the equipment—including per-incident repair and maintenance costs directly necessitated by SR&ED experimentation—can qualify as SR&ED overhead and other expenditures if properly isolated and documented.
Reliance on Arbitrary Allocation Methodologies and Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation

Even where an expenditure category is potentially capable of harbouring an incremental SR&ED component—such as shared utility consumption, specialized consumable supplies, or dual-role support personnel—the taxpayer in Imapro Corp. was not faulted for its evidence or its allocation method: the facts were largely set out in an agreed statement of facts supplemented by witness testimony, the Court accepted the 47.3 per cent floor-area apportionment as reasonable for the capital construction costs, and the current expenditures failed on the statutory thresholds rather than for lack of documentation; contemporaneous empirical evidence is nonetheless central to the CRA's current administrative approach. Under Canadian tax litigation principles, the taxpayer bears the initial evidentiary burden of demolishing the Minister's assumptions of fact supporting a Notice of Reassessment. As codified in the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, the method used by a claimant to allocate overhead and other expenditures to SR&ED must be reasonable, must be fully explainable by the claimant, and must be backed by objective support for the allocation; any method that arbitrarily connects the expenditures with the SR&ED work is disallowed.

Applying a flat corporate financial ratio—such as the percentage of SR&ED engineering headcount to total corporate headcount, or the ratio of direct SR&ED wages to total corporate payroll—to general ledger expense accounts fails to prove actual causal consumption by the SR&ED activities. Without contemporaneous time-tracking logs, equipment usage logs, utility sub-metering, or vendor invoices tied to specific experimental work orders, the Tax Court of Canada cannot verify whether the claimed fraction represents true incremental SR&ED expenditure or disguised general business overhead.
Failure to Demarcate Eligible SR&ED Prosecution from Pre-SR&ED, Commercial, and Post-SR&ED Activities

Disputes under section 37 of the ITA and section 2900 of the ITR frequently arise because taxpayers conflate the commercial lifecycle of a technology product with the strict statutory boundaries of SR&ED prosecution. Under CRA administrative policy (a matter not addressed in Imapro), technical and support expenditures are disqualified whenever they occur outside the strict temporal and technical perimeter of systematic experimentation. Prior to the commencement of eligible SR&ED, commercial and legal activities such as bidding on customer contracts, initiating and closing technology licensing agreements, and conducting non-technological feasibility studies (including assessing the commercial feasibility of a given technology or evaluating potential SR&ED collaborations) are excluded as regular business overhead.

During and after technical development, expenditures related to patent applications (including patent agent and legal work), the commercialization of existing intellectual property, sales, marketing, advertising, and attendance at general industry conventions or conferences do not resolve technological uncertainty through systematic experiment or analysis and are excluded from the SR&ED pool as ordinary business expenses under Section 3.1.2 of the CRA's policy. Similarly, routine commercial production (other than materials or equipment used in SR&ED), standard shipping and distribution of commercial products (as opposed to the shipping and distribution costs of experimental products strictly for internal or customer testing), and post-project ramp-down periods that are not part of systematic analysis fail to qualify. In the realm of human resources, expenses incurred to select and hire SR&ED personnel—specifically headhunter fees, recruitment advertising, travel costs related to the employment selection process, immigration costs (such as work permits or visas), and taxable employee benefits related to housing losses—are deductible only as regular business expenses and neither enter the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool nor earn ITCs. Conversely, moving expenses related to relocating selected candidates or existing SR&ED employees to another facility within Canada can be included in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and qualify for ITCs if proven to be directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED.
Contractual and Personnel Characterization Pitfalls

Finally, although this report draws on Imapro Corp. v. The Queen, [1992] 2 C.T.C. 298, that decision did not address the characterization of personnel; Canadian employment and tax jurisprudence more generally underscores the legal importance of accurate contractual characterization between employment relationships (contract of service) and independent contractor arrangements (contract for services) under the Income Tax Act and Canada Pension Plan regime. In the SR&ED context, misclassifying personnel has severe statutory repercussions for both direct wage claims and overhead calculations. Only employees of the taxpayer qualify to have their direct SR&ED salaries and wages included on Line 300/305 or their incremental support wages included on Line 360 of Form T661, and only eligible direct employee salaries form the salary base for calculating the Prescribed Proxy Amount under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR. Conversely, payments to arm's-length Canadian subcontractors performing SR&ED on the taxpayer's behalf are restricted to 80% inclusion for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9) of the ITA and cannot be used to generate proxy overhead. Moreover, where customer contracts or funding arrangements provide contract payments, government assistance, or reimbursement for technical development, subsection 127(18) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the ITA mandate that the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool be reduced by the amount of such assistance or contract payments.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement discussed in Imapro Corp. v. The Queen, [1992] 2 C.T.C. 298 (92 DTC 6487) and the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy against typical evidentiary or structural failures and the corresponding standard of proof; apart from the maintenance and upkeep of common areas, the failures listed are drawn from the CRA's policy and were not findings made against the taxpayer in Imapro.

headers: The Court's & CRA's Standard of Proof

cells: ITA s. 37(1)(a) & ITR s. 2900(1) (now ITA s. 248(1))

Eligible SR&ED Prosecution: Activities must constitute a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis to resolve technological uncertainty and achieve technological advancement.

Blending pre-project commercial feasibility studies, contract bidding, licensing negotiations, patent filing work, budget reviews, and post-experimentation ramp-down or commercial production with technical R&D.

Contemporaneous technical documentation proving a baseline technological uncertainty, explicit hypotheses, systematic experimental testing logs, and clear temporal demarcation excluding commercial, legal, and routine production phases.
ITR s. 2900(2)(c) & s. 2900(3)(b) — Prong 1

"Directly Related" Linkage Test: Overhead and other expenditures must connect directly—with no intervening step or intermediary—to (1) the SR&ED work, (2) the SR&ED staff, or (3) the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.

Claiming "overhead on overhead"—such as benefits of indirect support staff, HR/benefits program development, general legal/accounting fees, and general conference attendance—or earning ITCs on prescribed expenditures such as interest expenses and SR&ED claim preparation fees.

Unbroken, single-step causal trace proving the expenditure acts directly upon the SR&ED work, SR&ED personnel, or SR&ED equipment without passing through an intermediate corporate or administrative cost centre.
ITR s. 2900(2)(c) & s. 2900(3)(b) — Prong 2

Incremental ("But-For") Test: The expenditure, or the claimed portion thereof, would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED (or the provision of SR&ED premises/facilities/equipment) not occurred.

Claiming fixed general corporate expenses, baseline facility leases, common-area upkeep, fixed-cost equipment maintenance contracts, and post-SR&ED scrap/waste disposal that exist regardless of active SR&ED prosecution.

Empirical proof of "but-for" variability: vendor contracts, sub-metered utility records, or per-incident work orders demonstrating that the exact cost arose solely due to SR&ED activity and would equal zero in its absence.
ITR s. 2900(3)(a) & ITA s. 37(1)(a)

Maintenance & Upkeep of Premises, Facilities, or Equipment: Deductible where the premises, facility, or equipment is attributable "all or substantially all" (≥90%) to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or where specific upkeep costs are incremental.

Claiming a pro-rata share of general facility maintenance and the light, power, water, property tax, and telephone costs of common areas in a multi-use commercial and R&D building that fails the 90% dedication threshold and lacks incremental cost isolation.

Proof via floor-plan dedication logs and access controls that ≥90% of the facility/equipment use is SR&ED, or itemized invoices proving that specific maintenance/upkeep tasks were triggered strictly by SR&ED wear-and-tear.
ITR s. 2900(2)(b)–(c) — Allocation Methodology
Reasonable, Non-Arbitrary Allocation: Where an expenditure serves both SR&ED and non-SR&ED functions, the allocation methodology must reasonably and accurately measure the incremental SR&ED portion.
Applying arbitrary accounting formulas—such as multiplying general ledger overhead accounts by the ratio of R&D headcount or R&D salaries to total corporate payroll—without empirical usage data.
Contemporaneous time sheets, machine-hour logs, sub-metering data, and work-order tracking that establish a direct, verifiable physical or operational measure of SR&ED consumption.
ITR s. 2900(2)(b)–(c) — Staffing, Hiring & Relocation
Direct Engagement vs. Recruitment Exclusions: Only salaries of employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED (and incremental domestic relocation costs of SR&ED staff) qualify.
Claiming headhunter fees, recruitment advertising, interview travel, immigration/visa fees, and taxable housing-loss benefits, or misclassifying independent contractors as employees.

Executed employment contracts (contracts of service), task-level time tracking, and strict segregation of excluded recruitment/immigration costs from eligible domestic SR&ED employee relocation expenses.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian corporate taxpayers and their legal and technical advisors can proactively structure SR&ED claims to withstand CRA audit scrutiny under the Imapro Corp. v. The Queen standard, the following two industry case studies examine realistic audit failures and provide step-by-step remedial architectures.
Case Study 1: Advanced Photonics and Semiconductor Wafer-Inspection Hardware Manufacturer (OptiScan Systems Inc. — Ottawa, Ontario)
Industry Context and Initial Audit Exposure

OptiScan Systems Inc. ("OptiScan") is an Ottawa-based Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) developing ultra-high-resolution deep-ultraviolet (DUV) laser-scanning and interferometric wafer-inspection systems for semiconductor fabrication. Seeking to overcome severe optical aberration and thermal lens distortion at sub-10-nanometre inspection resolutions, OptiScan elected to use the Traditional Method on Form T661 rather than the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) because its specialized cleanroom consumables, optical bench recalibrations, high-voltage power consumption, and dedicated technical support costs substantially exceeded 55% of its direct SR&ED salary base.

Upon joint audit by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer (FR), OptiScan faced a proposed disallowance of $680,000 in claimed SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 and $240,000 in technical salaries, explicitly citing Imapro Corp. v. The Queen (92 DTC 6487; [1992] 2 C.T.C. 298) and the CRA SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy. Specifically, OptiScan had claimed 70% of a $180,000 annual fixed-fee service and preventive maintenance agreement with a third-party vendor for its excimer laser and electron-beam metrology suite based on an estimated 70% SR&ED utilization rate, which the CRA disallowed as a fixed, non-incremental expense. Furthermore, occupying a 40,000-square-foot facility in Kanata housing corporate headquarters, commercial assembly, and an optical R&D laboratory, OptiScan had multiplied its total building lease, property taxes, general hydro bill, and common-area janitorial expenses by the ratio of R&D headcount to total company headcount (62%), which the CRA rejected as an arbitrary allocation of fixed facility overhead. In addition, engineering project hours included pre-project commercial feasibility presentations for a prospective defence client, patent drafting sessions with external patent counsel, and a $45,000 hazardous fluoride gas purging and scrap-wafer disposal invoice incurred four months after the experimental optical trials had concluded. Finally, OptiScan improperly claimed $65,000 in executive headhunter fees and work-permit immigration legal costs for two optical physicists recruited from overseas, alongside the employer-paid health and dental benefits of two inventory clerks who provided indirect support to the R&D laboratory.
Step 1: Project Governance and Lifecycle Phase-Gate Demarcation

To cure the contamination of eligible SR&ED prosecution with commercial, legal, and post-project activities, OptiScan restructures its internal R&D project governance around four formal, auditable Phase Gates mapped directly to subsection 248(1) and section 37 of the ITA. Gate 0 designates a Pre-SR&ED Commercial and Non-Technological Feasibility phase tracked under excluded cost centre CC-100, into which all customer bidding, commercial return-on-investment modelling, licensing negotiations, and high-level literature reviews conducted prior to identifying a specific technological uncertainty are routed and permanently excluded from Form T661. Gate 1 marks the formal Commencement of SR&ED Prosecution under eligible cost centre SR-200, which can be opened only upon the formal sign-off of a Technological Uncertainty Charter by the Vice-President of Optical Engineering documenting why standard optical physics models and commercially available DUV lenses cannot prevent thermal wavefront distortion above 400 Watts of laser duty cycle.

Gate 2 governs Active Experimental Development and Concurrent Waste Disposal within eligible cost centre SR-200, encompassing all experimental design, prototype fabrication, optical bench testing, and analysis. Crucially, OptiScan amends its standard operating procedures to mandate that all hazardous excimer gas purging and contaminated silicon substrate disposal occur concurrently within the active testing sprint prior to Gate 3 sign-off, satisfying the CRA policy requirement that waste disposal costs be incurred while the SR&ED activity is actively prosecuted rather than after the SR&ED activity has finished. Gate 3 triggers SR&ED Termination, Intellectual Property Protection, and Commercial Ramp-Down under excluded cost centre CC-300; once the experimental hypothesis is validated or abandoned, Gate 3 locks cost centre SR-200 so that all subsequent patent application drafting, patent agent consultations, commercial pre-production engineering, and post-project ramp-down activities are strictly segregated from the SR&ED claim.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking Architecture

To overcome evidentiary objections regarding the systematic nature of its investigation and the reasonableness of its cost allocations, OptiScan replaces retrospective year-end narratives with a contemporaneous Hypothesis-Experiment-Analysis-Conclusion (HEAC) repository integrated directly into its engineering Jira and Confluence environment. Every experimental trial is assigned a unique SR-200 sub-ticket linking the specific technological uncertainty—such as micro-thermal refractive index drift in calcium fluoride (CaF₂) lens elements under 4 kHz pulsed DUV irradiation—to a quantified scientific hypothesis, such as testing whether active acoustic-wave phase conjugation coupled with asymmetric helium micro-channel cooling can constrain wavefront error below λ/20 RMS. Automated telemetry from the optical interferometers logs every test iteration, parameter adjustment, and failure mode with immutable timestamps, directly linking machine hours, consumable optical coatings destroyed, and engineer hours to the specific experimental sub-ticket without relying on retrospective estimates.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring for Equipment Maintenance, Personnel Recruitment, and Prototype Shipping

To overcome the CRA's policy-based incrementality bar on fixed-cost maintenance agreements and staffing expenses, OptiScan's tax counsel restructures vendor and employment agreements prior to the start of the taxation year. First, OptiScan renegotiates its third-party excimer laser service contract into an unbundled Two-Tier Master Service Agreement (MSA). Tier A establishes a minimal baseline annual inspection fee covering routine commercial readiness, which OptiScan deducts solely as a regular business expense under section 9 of the ITA. Tier B establishes Per-Incident and Usage-Metered Experimental Support Work Orders, billed exclusively per pulse-million or per optical realignment event triggered by high-energy SR&ED stress tests under project code SR-200. Because each Tier B invoice is legally and factually triggered only when an SR&ED experiment runs—and would equal zero had the SR&ED prosecution not occurred—it satisfies both the "directly related" and "incremental" tests of paragraph 2900(3)(b) of the ITR.

Second, OptiScan removes all headhunter fees, recruitment advertising, candidate interview travel, and immigration work-permit legal fees from Form T661, deducting them as regular business expenses. Conversely, for a senior optical scientist relocated from OptiScan's Vancouver satellite lab to the Ottawa cleanroom specifically to lead project SR-200, the employment addendum explicitly documents that the physical transfer within Canada is mandated solely for the prosecution of SR-200, rendering the domestic moving expenses eligible as an incremental SR&ED overhead expenditure under CRA policy. Third, where experimental DUV sensor sub-assemblies are shipped to a partner semiconductor foundry in Bromont, Quebec solely for destructive beta validation under real-world cleanroom conditions, the shipping contract and commercial bill of lading explicitly designate the cargo as a non-commercial experimental prototype shipped strictly for SR&ED validation testing under Project SR-200, qualifying the freight and transit insurance costs under the CRA policy exception for shipping experimental products for internal or customer testing.
Step 4: Empirical Overhead and Facility Cost Accounting (Line 360 Compliance)

To eliminate arbitrary headcount prorating and "overhead on overhead" under subsections 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3) of the ITR, OptiScan overhauls its facility and support cost accounting. OptiScan installs dedicated digital electrical sub-meters, chilled-water flow meters, and ultra-pure nitrogen mass-flow controllers on the SR-200 optical test cells; rather than claiming 62% of the building's general utility bill, OptiScan claims only the exact kilowatt-hours and nitrogen volumes consumed during logged SR-200 experimental runs above the baseline idle load. Furthermore, OptiScan physically partitions the 8,000-square-foot Class 100 Cleanroom Zone B with keycard access logs proving that 96% of total entry hours and equipment operating hours within Zone B are dedicated to SR-200 SR&ED prosecution, satisfying the "all or substantially all" (90% or greater) threshold under paragraph 2900(3)(a) of the ITR for cleanroom HEPA filter replacements and specialized environmental upkeep, while abandoning any claim for common areas, lobbies, or general office lease costs. Finally, for the two inventory and laboratory clerks who provide incremental support to SR-200 (such as preparing chemical etchants and logging experimental optical mounts), OptiScan tracks their exact hours via daily work-order logs and claims only that incremental portion of their base salaries on Line 360, while strictly excluding their related employee benefits, which represent disallowed "overhead on overhead" due to their indirect link to the SR&ED work.
Case Study 2: Industrial Bioprocessing and Automated Fermentation Control Software Developer (BioKinetics Process Technologies Ltd. — Mississauga, Ontario)
Industry Context and Initial Audit Exposure

BioKinetics Process Technologies Ltd. ("BioKinetics") is a Mississauga-based industrial biotechnology and process-control engineering firm that manufactures commercial enzyme formulations while conducting concurrent SR&ED to develop novel machine-learning (ML) Raman-spectroscopy sensor-fusion algorithms and anaerobic bioreactor impeller geometries. BioKinetics operates a dual-use industrial facility where commercial fermentation batches and experimental scale-up trials share plant infrastructure.

During a joint technical and financial review by the CRA, BioKinetics' SR&ED claim faced comprehensive adjustments grounded in Imapro Corp. v. The Queen. First, BioKinetics had claimed 45% of its plant steam generation, municipal water, wastewater treatment, and general plant maintenance expenses under subsection 2900(3) of the ITR based on the ratio of experimental fermentation batches to total annual batches, failing to prove that general plant maintenance and baseline steam generation were incremental to the SR&ED trials. Second, BioKinetics allocated a percentage of its central IT department, human resources department (including work on a new R&D employee retention benefits package), corporate accounting salaries, SR&ED tax consultant claim-preparation fees, and interest expense on its operating line of credit to Line 360 of Form T661, all of which the CRA disallowed either as prescribed expenditures ineligible for ITCs or as "overhead on overhead". Third, BioKinetics conducted several scale-up runs on its 5,000-litre commercial fermenters where the resulting enzyme output was sold to commercial customers, and it received milestone payments under a joint development agreement with an agricultural conglomerate without deducting those contract payments from its qualified SR&ED expenditure pool or segregating commercial production costs. Fourth, BioKinetics included payments to three incorporated independent software consultants in its direct employee salary base on Line 300 and attempted to allocate overhead based on their fees, violating the employment characterization requirements of the Income Tax Act.
Step 1: Project Governance and Dual-Use Facility Segregation

To prevent commercial fermentation operations from contaminating experimental bioprocessing trials, BioKinetics implements a binding Experimental Trial Isolation Protocol (ETIP) across its Mississauga plant. Before any bioreactor vessel is transitioned from commercial enzyme production to SR&ED experimentation, the Scientific Director must issue a formal Experimental Campaign Authorization (ECA). The ECA locks out commercial batch scheduling on that specific bioreactor line, defines the specific technological uncertainty—such as non-linear shear-stress cell lysis and dissolved-oxygen mass-transfer collapse when scaling recombinant mycelial broths from 50-litre pilot vessels to 5,000-litre industrial geometry—and establishes that the trial is not routine quality control or commercial production. Where an experimental fermentation run yields incidental commercially salable enzyme product, the costs of the run are rigorously bifurcated between incremental experimental sensor-fusion testing and standard commercial feedstock costs, ensuring that commercial production expenses (other than materials consumed or transformed directly in SR&ED under paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR) are excluded from the claim.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Algorithmic Experimentation Tracking

To substantiate the substantive eligibility of both the bioprocess engineering and the machine-learning sensor-fusion software development under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, BioKinetics links its Git version-control repositories and bioreactor Distributed Control System (DCS) historian databases directly to its ECA numbers. Software commits are tagged with specific algorithmic hypotheses addressing why conventional proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control loops and standard chemometric Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression models fail to resolve fluorescence background interference in high-turbidity fermentation broths. Failed neural-network training epochs, spectral signal-to-noise divergence logs, and empirical bioreactor crash data are archived contemporaneously alongside biochemist bench notebooks, demonstrating a structured, systematic investigation by means of experiment and analysis rather than routine software debugging or commercial plant optimization.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring of Customer Agreements, Subcontractors, and Maintenance

BioKinetics overhauls its external commercial, subcontractor, and maintenance contracts to align with the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy. In its customer agreements with the agricultural conglomerate, BioKinetics legally separates commercial enzyme supply contracts from its internal R&D program, stipulating that BioKinetics retains 100% ownership of all background and foreground intellectual property, bears full financial and technical risk for experimental algorithm development, and receives payment strictly for delivered commercial-grade product meeting standard specifications, thereby preventing commercial purchase orders from tainting the unfunded SR&ED expenditure pool.

Addressing its technical workforce under the common-law and statutory tests of employment recognized in Canadian tax jurisprudence (contract of service versus contract for services), BioKinetics converts two core full-time algorithm developers from independent contractors into salaried T4 employees under formal employment agreements, allowing their direct SR&ED wages to be claimed on Line 300 and included in the salary base for overhead proxy calculations. The remaining arm's-length corporate subcontractor is governed by a dedicated Statement of Work (SOW) explicitly detailing the SR&ED work performed in Canada on BioKinetics' behalf, claimed strictly as an arm's-length contract expenditure (subject to the 80% ITC inclusion rule under subsection 127(9) of the ITA) and excluded from employee wage and overhead calculations. Furthermore, general plant maintenance contracts are removed from the SR&ED claim; whenever an ECA requires custom fabrication of experimental baffle inserts, non-standard clean-in-place (CIP) sterilization cycles between toxic experimental runs, or optical sensor-port welding on a bioreactor vessel, outside millwrights and instrumentation technicians bill under separate Incremental SR&ED Work Orders specifying the ECA number and describing the exact experimental modification, establishing "but-for" incrementality under paragraphs 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(b) of the ITR.
Step 4: Granular Time Tracking and Strategic Election of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)

Finally, BioKinetics executes a quantitative statutory optimization between the Traditional Method and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method under subsection 37(8) of the ITA and subsection 2900(4) of the ITR. Under Sections 3.1, 4.8, and 5.2 of the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, BioKinetics recognizes that its interest expenses, corporate accounting, general legal fees, HR benefits program administration, SR&ED claim-preparation fees, and central IT department costs are either prescribed expenditures that earn no ITCs (interest expenses and claim-preparation fees) or disallowed as policy exclusions or "overhead on overhead". Moreover, because BioKinetics' shared Mississauga manufacturing plant cannot satisfy the 90% "all or substantially all" dedication threshold for facility upkeep under paragraph 2900(3)(a) of the ITR, only discrete, sub-metered utility spikes and per-incident experimental reconfiguration costs would survive audit under the Traditional Method.

By converting its core software developers into T4 employees and implementing granular daily time-tracking that captures every direct engineering and biochemical hour spent undertaking, supervising, or directly supporting SR&ED under paragraph 2900(2)(b) of the ITR, BioKinetics expands its eligible direct SR&ED salary base and formally elects the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method on Form T661 for the taxation year. Through this election, BioKinetics automatically generates a notional SR&ED overhead amount equal to 55% of its eligible SR&ED salary base for ITC calculation purposes without having to litigate shared plant utility allocations on Line 360, while continuing to deduct all ordinary facility, maintenance, and administrative overhead expenses in computing its regular business income under section 9 of the ITA.
Comparative Summary of Pre-Restructuring Audit Exposure vs. Post-Restructuring Compliance

cells: Equipment Maintenance & Calibration (OptiScan)
Claimed 70% of a fixed-cost annual laser maintenance contract based on estimated usage ratio; disallowed as non-incremental fixed cost.
Restructured into a Two-Tier MSA: fixed baseline fee deducted under ITA s. 9; per-incident experimental recalibration and pulse-metered overages billed on separate SR-200 work orders.
Imapro Corp. v. The Queen, 92 DTC 6487 (cited by the CRA for common-area costs, not maintenance contracts); ITR s. 2900(3)(b); CRA SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy s. 3.2 & s. 5.2.
Facility Upkeep & Utilities (OptiScan & BioKinetics)
Allocated general building rent, property tax, common areas, and plant utilities using arbitrary headcount or batch ratios.
Partitioned dedicated Class 100 Cleanroom (≥90% SR&ED logged use) and installed digital sub-meters on experimental test cells; elected PPA where facility is dual-use.
Imapro Corp. v. The Queen, [1992] 2 C.T.C. 298; ITA s. 37(1)(a), s. 37(8); ITR s. 2900(3)(a)–(b).
Support Staff, Benefits & Corporate Admin (OptiScan & BioKinetics)
Claimed central IT, HR, finance, claim-prep fees, interest, and benefits of indirect support staff ("overhead on overhead").
Excluded all corporate admin, interest, and claim-prep costs; claimed only time-logged incremental base wages of direct SR&ED support staff on Line 360 while excluding their indirect benefits.
Imapro Corp. v. The Queen, 92 DTC 6487 (did not address support staff, benefits, or administrative overhead); ITR s. 2900(2)(c); CRA SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy s. 3.1 & s. 4.8.
Project Lifecycle, IP & Waste Disposal (OptiScan)
Blended pre-SR&ED bidding/feasibility, patent legal work, and post-project hazardous scrap disposal into SR&ED pool.
Enforced 4-stage Phase Gates (CC-100, SR-200, CC-300); executed hazardous gas/wafer disposal concurrently during active SR-200 experimentation prior to project closure.
ITA s. 37(1)(a), s. 248(1); ITR s. 2900(2)(c); CRA SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (waste disposal & feasibility rules).
Personnel Hiring, Relocation & Contractors (OptiScan & BioKinetics)
Claimed headhunter fees, visa costs, and misclassified independent contractors as Line 300 employees.
Excluded all recruitment and immigration costs; isolated incremental domestic employee relocation; converted key developers to T4 contracts of service and isolated arm's-length SOWs.
Imapro Corp. v. The Queen, [1992] 2 C.T.C. 298 (did not address hiring, relocation, or contractor status); ITA s. 37(1), s. 127(9); CRA SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy s. 4.5.

body.text: Conclusion and Practice Recommendations for Canadian Tax Advisors

The ruling of the Federal Court—Trial Division in Imapro Corp. v. The Queen, [1992] 2 C.T.C. 298 (92 DTC 6487) confirmed that the Act permits a reasonable apportionment of SR&ED expenditures relating to a multi-purpose building, allowing a 47.3 per cent portion of the capital construction costs of common and administrative areas while upholding the disallowance of the corresponding portion of current maintenance and upkeep costs, which was neither all or substantially all attributable nor directly attributable to SR&ED. For Canadian tax counsel, chief financial officers, and engineering directors, the decision, read together with the CRA's current SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, supports three operational principles under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations. First, although Imapro accepted a reasonable floor-space apportionment of capital construction costs, it held that a floor-space share of current common-area costs is not directly attributable to SR&ED, and the CRA's current policy gives little weight to allocations of indirect current overhead by headcount, floor space, or payroll ratios under paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the ITR unless they are reasonable, explainable, and objectively supported. Second, any expenditure separated from the SR&ED work, SR&ED staff, or SR&ED equipment by an intervening administrative layer constitutes disallowed "overhead on overhead" and must be systematically stripped from Line 360 claims. Third, where a claimant elects to file under the Traditional Method rather than the Prescribed Proxy Amount method, commercial contracts for equipment maintenance, utilities, waste disposal, and technical support must be legally unbundled prior to the taxation year-end so that variable, SR&ED-triggered expenses are separately invoiced, contemporaneously tracked, and demonstrably incremental to the systematic investigation of technological uncertainty.

outcome: Appeal allowed in part; a 47.3% floor-area apportionment of capital costs was accepted, but common-area upkeep costs were not SR&ED.
